Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The author uses vivid, real-time scenes—such as the arrival in the kitchen, lunch on the porch, the trip to the nursery, and the hospital visit—to showcase the dynamic between Paul and his mother through sharp dialogue and sensory details. At the same time, summary and exposition are woven seamlessly into the narrative to provide essential background information (like the father's death and the narrator's life in Brooklyn) and to compress time effectively, particularly during the month-long transition between the May visit and the June heatwave. This balance keeps the pacing smooth while ensuring the emotional core of the story feels immediate and earned.
